entry.title: Volvo EX30 Owner Pays 4c per Km
entry.summary: Consumer interest in electric vehicles in South Africa is accelerating, and one of the most compelling data sets presented at a recent industry webinar came not from a research institution but from the personal driving…
entry.content:
Consumer interest in electric vehicles in South Africa is accelerating, and one of the most compelling data sets presented at a recent industry webinar came not from a research institution but from the personal driving record of a Volvo Cars South Africa customer.

Grant Locke, Managing Director of Volvo Car South Africa, used his address at the EE Business Intelligence webinar in May to share two years of granular charging data from a customer's Volvo EX30, offering private motorists an unusually transparent window into the real cost of everyday electric vehicle ownership in South Africa.

Over a period from March 2024 to March 2026, the customer covered 28,744 kilometres across 188 charging sessions, consuming a total of 4,991 kilowatt-hours of energy. Of those sessions, 179 drew on excess home solar generation or free workplace charging. Just nine sessions were paid for, with total charging costs over the full two-year period amounting to a mere R970.

"The average cost per kilometre for an EV charging at home or at work, assuming 90 percent or more of charging off excess home solar, works out at around four cents per kilometre," Locke told the audience.

By comparison, the same distance driven in a petrol vehicle consuming 7.5 litres per 100 kilometres at R22.40 per litre would have cost an estimated R48,277 in fuel. After deducting the EX30's total charging bill of R970, Locke calculated that the motorist's vehicle had avoided approximately R47,307 in fuel costs over those two years.

Locke's data showed that the EX30 produced a blended emissions intensity of around 106 grams of CO2 per kilometre, against a petrol equivalent of 237.5 grams per kilometre when accounting for fuel extraction and refining. The net result was approximately 3,777 kilograms of CO2 avoided across the two-year period, representing a reduction of roughly 55 percent against a comparable petrol vehicle.

Consumer interest is tracking the numbers

Locke supported the financial case with evidence of rising consumer attention. Google search data for electric car-related keywords in South Africa showed a search index of 37 in the first half of the measured period, rising to 65 in the second half, pointing to a near-doubling of online interest over twelve months. Traffic to the Volvocars.com/za website told a similar story, with BEV product page sessions overtaking petrol model sessions in March and April 2026 for the first time.

On the question of total cost of ownership, Locke acknowledged that South Africa had not yet reached the straightforward position seen in some mature markets. The International Energy Agency's Global EV Outlook 2026 states that electric cars often carry a lower total cost of ownership than ICE vehicles over a vehicle lifetime.

In South Africa, Locke said the picture remained more nuanced. Purchase prices for EVs remain higher than their petrol equivalents, partly as a result of import duties. Operating and maintenance costs are clearly lower, while the residual value question is still developing as the secondhand market matures. Tyre costs and insurance premiums were flagged as areas where EVs may carry a marginal disadvantage at present.

Public charging infrastructure is improving rapidly

Locke also presented data on public charging progress that will reassure private motorists considering longer journeys. Major highway corridors including the N1, N2 and N3 now have charge points spaced within approximately 300 kilometres. In Johannesburg, Cape Town and Durban, a public charge point can be located within 20 kilometres.

Charging speeds are advancing quickly as well. Locke described a first-hand test conducted on 21 May 2026 at the Zero Carbon Charge station at Three Towers on the N3, where a Volvo ES90 charged from 9 percent to 79 percent in just over 20 minutes, achieving a peak charging speed of 321 kilowatts. The session delivered approximately 67 kilowatt-hours and added around 400 kilometres of range.

Rubicon's network data showed that total public charging sessions doubled in 2024 relative to 2023, with early 2026 figures already running 64 percent ahead of the same period last year.

Looking beyond the individual ownership experience, Locke pointed to the emerging capability of bidirectional charging as a development that could fundamentally reshape the relationship between electric vehicles and the home energy system, allowing owners to power appliances, back up the home during outages, and in time, feed surplus energy back into the grid.

entry.title: Electric Fleets Cross Competitive Cost Thresholds
entry.summary: South African commercial fleet operators that have made the switch to electric vehicles are recording measurable savings across fuel, maintenance and total cost of ownership (TCO), according to data presented by Ndia Magadagela, CEO of…
entry.content:
South African commercial fleet operators that have made the switch to electric vehicles are recording measurable savings across fuel, maintenance and total cost of ownership (TCO), according to data presented by Ndia Magadagela, CEO of Everlectric, at a sector webinar hosted by EE Business Intelligence.

Drawing on a portfolio of real-world fleet deployments spanning more than 12.5 million kilometres of electric driving across clients including DSV, FedEx, Woolworths, Vodacom and Sanitech, Magadagela's presentation made a detailed financial case for commercial fleet electrification that goes well beyond environmental aspiration.

"Commercial fleets have done the maths," Magadagela told the audience of roughly 850 registered delegates. "They have seen that there are clearer economics. It is cheaper to run. And they have seen that it does not affect their downtime."

Those fleets have collectively saved an estimated 2.75 million kilograms of carbon emissions since deployment began, with Everlectric reporting 100 percent operational availability and zero mechanical downtime across its managed fleet.

Where the savings are found

The core of Magadagela's argument rested on a rigorous TCO analysis comparing the Maxus eDeliver3 electric panel van against the Isuzu D-Max across a modelled five-year lifecycle and 240,000 kilometres. 

On a direct purchase basis, the electric vehicle's TCO came in at R860,000 against R1.26 million for the equivalent ICE vehicle, a saving of approximately 27 percent. On a financed basis, the gap narrowed somewhat, with EV TCO at R1.04 million against R1.28 million for the ICE alternative, still representing a 23 percent advantage.

The figures account for the full cost base, including vehicle price, insurance, fuel versus electricity, service and maintenance, tyre costs, and residual value. Electric vehicles carry a higher upfront capital cost, with the Maxus eDeliver3 coming in at roughly 70 percent above its ICE equivalent before import duties are factored in. The savings, however, accumulate through dramatically lower operating costs.

Electricity costs in the analysis were modelled at R0.45 per kilometre for the EV against R2.41 per kilometre for the diesel vehicle, an efficiency gap of approximately 80 percent in favour of electric. 

Maintenance costs were calculated at R0.41 per kilometre for the EV against R0.76 per kilometre for the ICE vehicle, reflecting the significantly fewer moving parts in an electric powertrain. EVs also demonstrated a superior residual value in the model, with a projected return of R195,000 against R96,000 for the ICE equivalent.

"Additional savings are possible given that EV costing and efficiencies continue to improve," Magadagela noted, "with significant savings expected from 2025 technology."

The crossover point

A critical insight from the presentation was the identification of monthly kilometre thresholds at which operating an electric vehicle becomes cheaper than its diesel counterpart in a fully maintained lease structure. 

For the one-tonne segment, comparing the Maxus eDeliver3 against the Isuzu D-Max, Toyota Hilux and Volkswagen Caddy, the crossover point using 2025 cost data sits at approximately 3,200 kilometres per month. 

For the four-tonne segment, the Maxus eDeliver 75 outperforms all ICE competitors from around 2,500 kilometres per month. In the eight-tonne bracket, the same EV crossover dynamic applies at broadly similar thresholds.

A further comparison between the BYD Dolphin Surf and the Hyundai i10 Cargo, conducted using 2026 data, found a breakeven point of 2,685 kilometres per month, beyond which the electric vehicle is consistently the more affordable option to run.

The data also tested oil price sensitivity on the four-tonne segment. At a diesel price of R22 per litre, the eDeliver 75 becomes cheaper than the average diesel equivalent from around 2,500 kilometres per month. 

At R28 per litre, the crossover arrives earlier; at R35 per litre, the electric advantage widens substantially. Given the global trajectory of liquid fuel prices, Magadagela's sensitivity analysis suggested the EV case would only strengthen over time.

Removing barriers through a service model

Magadagela acknowledged that several structural challenges had historically slowed fleet electrification in South Africa, among them limited model availability, concerns about grid stability, prohibitive upfront capital costs, and the complexity of managing charging infrastructure. 

Everlectric's response has been to structure its offering as an electric vehicle as a service model, delivering the vehicle, dedicated on-site DC fast charging infrastructure, renewable electricity supply, full maintenance, and a cloud-based fleet management application under a single monthly invoice.

"This model allows an electric vehicle user or commercial fleet to use an electric vehicle, have charging infrastructure dedicated to them, have all their maintenance already worked into the solution, and have a driver-facing app that allows them to do their deliveries without the headache of knowing where to charge, when to charge, or when electricity is cheapest," she said.

The approach has proved particularly effective for hub-and-spoke operations, where vehicles return to a central depot for overnight or scheduled charging and predictable daily range requirements reduce range anxiety as a practical concern.

Magadagela said the availability of electric commercial vehicle models had improved considerably in recent years, spanning panel vans, trucks and passenger transport, reducing a barrier that would have prevented fleet adoption only a few years ago.

South Africa's advance in distributed solar generation had further reinforced the business case, with co-located solar and charging infrastructure now common across early adopter sites.

entry.title: SA Moves to Bolster EV Component Manufacturing

category.term: National Association of Automotive Component and Allied Manufacturers

entry.summary: Trade, industry and competition minister, Parks Tau, has published draft amendments to the Automotive Production and Development Programme (APDP) that would extend government incentives to a broader range of materials used in electric vehicle (EV)…
entry.content:
Trade, industry and competition minister, Parks Tau, has published draft amendments to the Automotive Production and Development Programme (APDP) that would extend government incentives to a broader range of materials used in electric vehicle (EV) manufacturing, with a particular focus on battery production.

The proposals, which are open for public comment, include increased production credits and customs rebates designed to encourage investment in high-value EV components on South African soil.

The changes build on the EV white paper published by the Department of Trade, Industry and Competition (DTIC) several years ago and represent the latest in a series of policy steps taken to develop a domestic new energy vehicle (NEV) ecosystem.

Renai Moothilal, CEO of the National Association of Automotive Component and Allied Manufacturers (NAACAM), welcomed the proposals. "It's a step in the right direction. It's definitely a positive move and building on what was outlined a couple of years ago in the EV white paper published by DTIC," he said.

Regional dimension

Moothilal noted that the incentives would apply across the Southern African Customs Union (SACU), giving the proposals a regional dimension that could have broader industrial significance. "It's applicable across SACU and in some way could give some real impetus to what we talk about when we say regional industrialisation," he said.

The draft amendments follow two earlier policy interventions. An additional cash incentive for NEV components was introduced two years ago, and last year's budget included a 150% accelerated depreciation allowance for electric vehicles produced in South Africa.

The China question

South Africa's efforts to grow its EV manufacturing base come against the backdrop of China's formidable dominance of the global EV market.

Chinese manufacturers, backed by close to two decades of targeted industrial policy and substantial state support, account for more than 60% of EVs sold globally, as well as a commanding share of key component production including batteries.

Moothilal acknowledged the scale of the challenge but argued that South Africa's approach of using tax-based incentives and customs rebates, rather than direct subsidies, was appropriate given the country's fiscal constraints.

He said the goal was to position South Africa and the wider region as investment destinations and technology partners for large Chinese and other international producers.

"The mineral advantages that the region has does give some credence to bringing on board some of the large Chinese component producers," he said, adding that new entrants preparing to enter the South African market were already exploring ways to localise high-value components.

Moothila said more could always be done, but expressed satisfaction that policy was moving forward. "It is good to see some of this coming across the line."

entry.title: SA Gets Dedicated Voice for Electric Mobility
entry.summary: The establishment of the South African Electric Mobility Association (SAEMA) marks a turning point for an industry that has long operated without a unified representative body. South Africa's electric vehicle sector has taken a significant…
entry.content:
The establishment of the South African Electric Mobility Association (SAEMA) marks a turning point for an industry that has long operated without a unified representative body.

South Africa's electric vehicle sector has taken a significant step towards organised advocacy with the formal announcement of the South African Electric Mobility Association, a body that will represent the full spectrum of stakeholders driving the country's transition to electric mobility.

The announcement was made by Hiten Parmar, executive director of The Electric Mission, during a high-profile webinar hosted by EE Business Intelligence on 26 May 2026.

Speaking to an audience of approximately 850 registered delegates drawn from government, industry and the broader automotive sector, Parmar described the association as a direct response to a gap that has hindered South Africa's ability to develop and advance a coherent electric mobility agenda.

"We are proud to announce the establishment of the South African Electric Mobility Association, which is really focusing on community engagement of all operators and actors in this space and really becoming a voice for advancing the electric mobility industry in South Africa," Parmar said.

The association will bring together manufacturers, importers, installers, charge point operators and EV drivers under a single representative structure, giving the sector the kind of organised presence that industries such as solar PV have used to engage policymakers and shape regulatory outcomes.

During the webinar, Parmar presented data showing that South Africa's battery electric vehicle stock, when corrected to include import data from the South African Revenue Service alongside national registration figures, stands at approximately 7,900 passenger units.

That figure is materially higher than the 4,502 units reflected in official registration data, pointing to a measurement gap that a properly resourced industry body is well placed to address.

A critical moment for policy

The association's establishment comes at a pivotal moment for South Africa's EV policy environment. Parmar noted that the government signalled a 150% tax rebate on manufacturing incentives for battery electric and fuel cell electric vehicles in March 2026, a development the sector has been watching closely as a potential catalyst for local production.

South Africa's automotive manufacturing sector produced 618,000 units in 2025, the overwhelming majority of them destined for export markets in the EU and the UK. Both markets are moving towards zero emission vehicle requirements within defined timelines, creating an urgent commercial imperative for South Africa to align its manufacturing incentives accordingly. Without that alignment, the country's century-old automotive industry risks losing access to its primary export destinations.

Parmar was direct about the scale of the challenge. South Africa is tracking behind comparable developing nations in EV adoption, and the absence of a unified industry voice has made coherent engagement with government on demand-side and supply-side policy mechanisms more difficult than it needs to be.

The South African Electric Mobility Association is positioned to change that. For an industry at a critical juncture, the arrival of a dedicated representative body may prove to be one of the most consequential developments of 2026.

entry.title: Why Chinese EVs Are Cheaper
entry.summary: Electric vehicles made in China consistently cost far less than comparable models produced elsewhere in the world. A new analysis from the IEA Global EV Outlook 2026 sheds light on the structural reasons behind this…
entry.content:
Electric vehicles made in China consistently cost far less than comparable models produced elsewhere in the world. A new analysis from the IEA Global EV Outlook 2026 sheds light on the structural reasons behind this price gap, and the findings are more nuanced than many observers might expect.

The most obvious explanation that comes to mind is government subsidies. China has indeed offered generous financial support to its EV industry over many years, and preferential financing helped Chinese manufacturers scale up their operations faster than their international rivals.

Subsidies have played a meaningful role in shaping the industry, and analysts acknowledge they likely still matter today. However, the IEA's findings make clear that subsidies alone are far from a sufficient explanation for the pricing gap that exists today.

Labour costs are another contributing factor. Building an internal combustion engine vehicle in China costs roughly 30 per cent less than doing so in Germany, and labour rates in China run approximately three to five times lower than in many advanced economies. This is a genuine advantage, though it too, tells only part of the story.

China's Battery Advantage 

The single most important reason Chinese EVs are cheaper comes down to batteries. Chinese manufacturers have spent well over a decade building deep expertise in every layer of battery production, from raw components and battery cells through to finished battery packs.

The scale of this accumulated knowledge is reflected in the numbers. Manufacturing efficiency alone accounts for more than 40 per cent of the battery production cost gap between China and Europe.

Chinese producers have also embraced lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, battery chemistry far more widely than manufacturers elsewhere. LFP batteries avoid the expensive nickel-based materials that remain standard in many Western and South Korean battery designs. The result is a cheaper battery that is also well suited to the mass-market vehicles that dominate Chinese EV sales.

Factory scale reinforces every one of these advantages. Some Chinese EV plants are now capable of producing over one million vehicles per year. At that volume, fixed costs shrink dramatically on a per-vehicle basis, and the efficiency gains that come with repetition compound across the entire supply chain.

One factor that turns out to matter far less than popular perception suggests is energy costs. Electricity and fuel expenses account for only one to four per cent of total vehicle manufacturing costs, meaning that cheaper power in China is a negligible contributor to the price difference.

For South African consumers and fleet buyers watching the global EV market, the implications are significant. Chinese brands are already arriving on local shores at price points that put EVs within reach of a far wider audience than before.

The IEA analysis suggests this is not a temporary phenomenon driven by political support alone. The scale, the supply chain integration, the battery leadership and the manufacturing experience that underpin Chinese EV pricing have taken years to build, and closing the gap will require other regions to invest seriously in the same foundations over the long term.

entry.title: Tata Motors Showcases Four Electric Commercial Vehicles
entry.summary: Tata Motors has placed electric mobility at the heart of its African commercial vehicle strategy, displaying four zero-emission vehicles at a showcase event in Cape Town. The event, held on 22 May, brought together 11…
entry.content:
Tata Motors has placed electric mobility at the heart of its African commercial vehicle strategy, displaying four zero-emission vehicles at a showcase event in Cape Town.

The event, held on 22 May, brought together 11 vehicles in total, but it was the electric quartet that drew the most attention, spanning last-mile delivery, urban freight, heavy cargo and mining applications.

The breadth of the electric line-up signals that Tata is moving well beyond pilot programmes and is positioning battery-electric vehicles as practical, revenue-generating tools for African fleet operators.

From city streets to construction sites

The smallest of the four electric vehicles, the Ace Pro EV, is a compact mini-truck designed for last-mile urban deliveries. Built around low total cost of ownership, it is aimed at operators seeking an affordable entry point into electric commercial transport without sacrificing the practicality needed for high-frequency city routes.

Stepping up in size and payload, the Intra EV is a fully electric pickup engineered for more demanding urban cargo duty cycles. Tata says the vehicle offers extended range alongside improved earning potential, making it a credible option for operators running dense urban delivery schedules where fuel and maintenance costs weigh heavily on margins.

The Ultra E.9 rounds out the urban freight offering. A light electric truck designed for intra-city logistics, it prioritises manoeuvrability and quiet operation, attributes that are increasingly valued as cities across Africa introduce stricter emissions and noise regulations in commercial zones.

Heavy-duty ambitions

The most significant vehicle in the electric line-up is arguably the Prima E28.K, a robust electric tipper aimed squarely at mining and construction fleets.

Fitted with a high-torque drivetrain and engineered for heavy-duty endurance, the Prima E28.K is Tata's clearest statement yet that zero-emission commercial transport is ready to move beyond urban logistics and into some of the most demanding operating environments on the continent.

Tata says the vehicle offers faster turnaround cycles than diesel equivalents, a claim that will resonate with mining operators for whom downtime carries significant financial consequences. The ability to decarbonise extraction and earthmoving operations without sacrificing productivity has been a long-standing challenge for the sector, and the Prima E28.K is positioned as a meaningful step towards resolving it.

Asif Shamim, Head of International Business at Tata Motors, noted that the portfolio was designed with real-world African conditions in mind. "The portfolio presented here demonstrates the range of platforms and technologies we are building across segments, including electric vehicles, tailored to different use cases and operating conditions," he said.

With seven assembly facilities across Africa and more than 320 service touchpoints on the continent, Tata Motors has the infrastructure to support electric vehicle adoption at scale, a factor that has historically held back EV uptake in markets where after-sales support remains limited.

entry.title: The Economics Of Charging Locations
entry.summary: The latest edition of the International Energy Agency's Global EV Outlook has taken a close look at one of the most frequently cited barriers to electric car ownership, namely the question of whether drivers need…
entry.content:
The latest edition of the International Energy Agency's Global EV Outlook has taken a close look at one of the most frequently cited barriers to electric car ownership, namely the question of whether drivers need access to home charging before they are willing to make the switch.

The short answer, according to the IEA, is that home charging is highly advantageous, though it remains far from the only viable option.

For drivers who are able to plug in at home overnight, the financial case for going electric is compelling. Home charging typically draws on residential electricity tariffs, which are considerably cheaper than public charging rates.

In the United States, for example, home charging can save a driver as much as $860 per year in operating costs compared to running a petrol vehicle. In the European Union, that saving sits at around $740, and in China it is roughly $620.

The picture shifts considerably for drivers who rely on public infrastructure. Slow public charging can cost up to 150% more than residential electricity, which chips away at the running-cost advantage that makes EVs so attractive. Fast charging, while increasingly convenient, can be so expensive that it wipes out the operational savings altogether.

Lessons From The Chinese Market

The IEA points to China as a striking example of how high EV adoption rates can be achieved even when home charging access is limited. China now holds the world's largest electric car stock at 44.3 million vehicles, and EV sales account for more than half of all new car sales.

Despite this, only around 52% of Chinese car owners have access to a home charger. In the European Union, where the electric car stock stands at 12.1 million, that figure rises to 80%, suggesting that home charging access and EV uptake do not always move in lockstep.

Part of the reason for this success is that most drivers simply do not need to charge every single day. The average private car covers between 30 and 70 kilometres daily, which is well within the range of a modern battery electric vehicle. Even taxi drivers, who typically cover between 150 and 250 kilometres per shift, are using only about half the average on-road range of a contemporary EV.

Workplace charging is growing steadily and offers a practical solution for commuters. Public overnight charging and curbside infrastructure are also expanding, alongside semi-private options such as chargers in shopping centre car parks.

Ultra-fast chargers, capable of delivering enough energy for several days of commuting in a single 20-minute session, are appearing at fuel stations, supermarkets, and retail locations, making them easier to fold into everyday routines.

The IEA argues that governments have a meaningful role to play in making these alternatives more affordable. India and Indonesia already regulate the electricity price applied to public EV charging, helping to keep tariffs closer to residential rates.

The IEA recommends that other governments consider similar measures, alongside targeted investment in charger deployment near multi-family housing and in underserved communities.

This message for South African policymakers and EV stakeholders is a timely one. As the country works to grow its own EV market, ensuring that charging access extends beyond those with private garages and dedicated parking will be central to making electric mobility a genuinely inclusive option.

entry.title: SA Explores Tax Incentive to Boost EV Uptake
entry.summary: A new study could pave the way for a salary sacrifice-style scheme that makes EVs more affordable for South African workers The African Climate Foundation (ACF), working in partnership with the Just Energy Transition Project…
entry.content:
A new study could pave the way for a salary sacrifice-style scheme that makes EVs more affordable for South African workers

The African Climate Foundation (ACF), working in partnership with the Just Energy Transition Project Management Unit (JET PMU) in The Presidency, has issued a call for proposals to conduct a rapid diagnostic evaluation of a potential tax incentive mechanism aimed at accelerating the uptake of new energy vehicles (NEVs) in South Africa.

The request for proposals, published under reference RFP-12-JET IP, invites qualified consultants and research consortia to assess whether South Africa's existing tax framework could be adapted to make electric vehicles significantly more accessible to private consumers — without placing additional strain on the national fiscus.

The Challenge Facing South Africa

South Africa's electric vehicle market has been slow to grow. High upfront purchase prices, combined with tight government finances, have made it difficult to introduce the kind of direct cash subsidies that have driven global EV adoption.

The transport sector currently accounts for approximately 14 per cent of the country's total greenhouse gas emissions, and the slow transition to cleaner vehicles is seen as a meaningful obstacle to meeting South Africa's climate commitments under the Just Energy Transition framework.

The ACF and JET PMU believe that an innovative, fiscally responsible policy lever may already exist within South Africa's tax legislation — and that it simply needs to be properly examined and designed.

Looking to the United Kingdom for Inspiration

The study draws inspiration from the United Kingdom's salary sacrifice scheme for zero-emission vehicles, a programme that has proven highly effective in accelerating EV adoption among employed workers.

Under such a scheme, employees agree to sacrifice a portion of their pre-tax salary in exchange for a benefit-in-kind — in this case, access to an electric vehicle. The arrangement reduces the employee's taxable income, lowers the overall cost of the vehicle, and provides employers with an attractive staff benefit at the same time.

South Africa already operates similar tax structures in other areas, including pension contributions and medical aid deductions, as well as allowances for the personal use of company vehicles. The diagnostic study will investigate whether these existing frameworks could be extended or adapted to support NEV uptake in a comparable way.

Norway is also cited as a relevant example, where company car allowances have played a significant role in driving widespread EV adoption across the population.

What the Study Will Cover

The successful service provider will be expected to deliver a comprehensive body of work over a 17-week period, running from June to September 2026. The assignment will cover five main areas of investigation.

The first phase will involve a comparative review of international EV tax incentive models, examining how schemes in countries such as the United Kingdom and Norway have been structured, what tax rates and vehicle value caps have been applied, and what lessons can be drawn for the South African context.

The second phase will assess South Africa's existing legislative and regulatory framework, including the Income Tax Act, the Tax Administration Act, and the Labour Relations Act, to identify which provisions would support or hinder the introduction of such a scheme, and what amendments would be required.

The third and most substantial phase will involve the development of an econometric and fiscal model to simulate the potential impacts of different scheme designs. This will include projections for government revenue, consumer savings across different income brackets, projected increases in NEV sales, and broader developmental outcomes such as job creation, infrastructure investment, and reductions in carbon emissions.

The fourth phase will bring together key stakeholders — including National Treasury, the South African Revenue Service, the Department of Trade, Industry and Competition, the National Association of Automobile Manufacturers of South Africa, leasing companies, and organised labour — to validate the findings and refine the proposed implementation roadmap.

The fifth and final phase will produce a summary report and presentation for the steering committee, which will be chaired by the JET NEV PMO and will include representatives from National Treasury, the Department of Transport, and the Presidency's Policy and Coordination Committee.

A Focus on Inclusion and Gender Equity

The evaluation has a strong emphasis on gender responsiveness and social inclusion. The study must assess how different scheme designs would affect women, youth, and persons with disabilities in different ways, and must apply an intersectional lens to understand how overlapping identities influence access to and benefit from any proposed incentive. The evaluation is required to achieve a Gender Responsive rating on the DPME Gender Results Effectiveness Scale.

Who Should Apply

The ACF is seeking proposals from teams that bring together expertise across tax law, labour law, economic and fiscal modelling, public policy, the automotive sector, stakeholder facilitation, and gender analysis. Proposals may be submitted by individual organisations or by consortia, provided that the full range of required skills is represented within a single submission.

Proposals must be submitted through the ACF portal and must include a technical proposal of no more than 12 pages, a signed conflict of interest declaration, a tax clearance certificate, company registration documents, and a completed pricing template. Submissions via email will not be accepted.

The deadline for queries is 25 May 2026 at 17h00 South African Standard Time. The deadline for proposal submissions is 1 June 2026 at 17h00 South African Standard Time.

Technical queries may be directed to Christel Jacob at the JET PMU via christel.jacob@jetpmu.org.za, with the subject line referencing RFP 12. Portal assistance is available through grants@africanclimatefoundation.org.

A Pivotal Moment for South Africa's EV Sector

If the diagnostic study finds that a salary sacrifice-style scheme is feasible and well-designed, it could represent a turning point for South Africa's electric vehicle market.

A well-structured tax incentive would lower the barrier to entry for thousands of employed South Africans, stimulate demand for locally manufactured NEVs, support the growth of the domestic automotive value chain, and contribute meaningfully to the country's decarbonisation goals — all without requiring direct government expenditure.

The findings of the study will be presented to the Interministerial Committee as an evidence-based proposal, with the potential to inform future tax amendments and policy frameworks that could reshape the trajectory of EV adoption in South Africa.

Proposals close 1 June 2026. For more information, visit the ACF portal under RFP-12-JET IP.

entry.title: Global EV Sales Surge to 20 Million Units
entry.summary: The global electric vehicle revolution reached a significant milestone in 2025, with worldwide sales exceeding 20 million units for the first time, representing one in every four new cars sold, according to the latest Global…
entry.content:
The global electric vehicle revolution reached a significant milestone in 2025, with worldwide sales exceeding 20 million units for the first time, representing one in every four new cars sold, according to the latest Global EV Outlook 2026 released by the International Energy Agency.

The landmark achievement arrives at a pivotal moment, as the ongoing energy crisis sparked by conflict in the Middle East forces governments and consumers alike to reconsider their reliance on imported oil.

The remarkable 20% year-on-year growth in electric car sales continues a trajectory that began in 2021, with annual increases of approximately 3.5 million vehicles each year. This sustained momentum has brought the global electric car fleet to around 5% of all vehicles on the road, collectively displacing 1.2 million barrels of oil per day in 2025 alone.

Europe Leads Growth Surge as Policy Frameworks Tighten

Among major markets, Europe experienced the most dramatic transformation in 2025. Electric car sales surged by more than 30% to surpass 4 million units, pushing the market share to 28% of total sales. This acceleration followed years of stagnation and came in direct response to stricter European Union CO2 standards for cars and vans that entered a new phase requiring a 15% reduction in emissions from new sales compared to 2021 levels.

The policy shift prompted automakers to adjust their pricing strategies and introduce more affordable electric vehicle models to comply with the new emissions targets. European manufacturers responded by expanding their electric offerings while continuing to face growing competition from Chinese imports, which accounted for almost 60% of electric cars imported into the European Union in 2025.

China Maintains Dominance Despite Slower Growth

China retained its position as the world's largest electric vehicle market, with nearly 55% of all new cars sold being electric. More than 13 million electric cars found buyers in the country during 2025, accounting for six out of every ten electric cars sold globally. However, growth rates moderated compared to the explosive expansion of previous years, partly due to the temporary suspension of the government's trade-in scheme in several cities during July 2025.

The Chinese market demonstrated remarkable price competitiveness, with 70% of battery electric cars sold in 2025 already cheaper than the average conventional car. In the small car segment, electric vehicles have effectively displaced conventional cars entirely, creating a market dynamic that pushes electric cars toward exceeding 90% of total car sales by 2035 according to the IEA's projections.

China's manufacturing prowess remained unchallenged, accounting for nearly 75% of electric cars produced globally in 2025. The country produced almost 22 million electric cars, representing a more than 25% increase over the previous year. Intense domestic competition squeezed profit margins, pushing manufacturers to seek opportunities overseas. Chinese electric car exports doubled to a record high of over 2.5 million units in 2025, with more than 35% of all Chinese car exports being electric vehicles, up from 20% in 2024.

United States Market Faces Policy Turbulence

The United States electric vehicle market experienced relative stagnation in 2025, with the sales share remaining just below 10% of total car sales. The year concluded with a significant downturn in the final quarter following the end of federal EV tax credits, highlighting the continued importance of policy support in driving adoption. The contrast between the stable overall year and the sharp decline at year's end underscored the sensitivity of the market to fiscal incentives.

Imports to the United States fell slightly in 2025, with the largest share coming from Mexico. The tightening of access to advanced manufacturing production tax credits posed challenges for Korean and Japanese battery manufacturers heavily exposed to the US market, potentially reshaping the competitive landscape in coming years.

Emerging Markets Drive Unexpected Growth

Perhaps the most surprising development of 2025 came from emerging markets, where electric vehicle adoption accelerated at rates exceeding even the established markets. Southeast Asia witnessed annual sales more than double to reach nearly 20% market share, led by impressive growth in Vietnam, Indonesia, and Thailand. Latin American sales grew by 75%, with Brazil and Mexico leading the charge.

More than 100 countries recorded electric car sales growth in 2025, and in one-third of these nations, electric vehicles represented at least 10% of new car sales. The availability of affordable Chinese-made electric cars played a crucial role in this expansion, bringing down prices and making electric mobility accessible to markets that previously seemed years away from meaningful adoption.

In Thailand, electric car prices reached parity with conventional vehicles two years ago, while Indonesia saw its average price premium for electric cars decline from over 50% in 2024 to around 40% in 2025. Vietnam emerged as the only country in Southeast Asia with a sizable domestic EV manufacturer offering vehicles at prices comparable to conventional cars, positioning it to potentially reach an electric car sales share of over 80% by 2035.

Energy Crisis Amplifies Economic Benefits of Electric Driving

The closure of the Strait of Hormuz due to conflict in the Middle East triggered a surge in crude oil and petroleum product prices globally, fundamentally altering the economic calculus for vehicle buyers. The crisis brought energy security and oil import dependency into sharp focus for many nations, with the road transport sector representing close to half of total oil demand.

Electric vehicles, with their significantly higher energy efficiency compared to conventional cars, offered immediate relief from escalating fuel costs. Based on average oil prices in April 2026, the annual fuel cost savings associated with driving an electric vehicle in the European Union grew 35% compared to 2025 savings. For corporate fleets covering long distances, the running cost advantages multiplied several times beyond those enjoyed by general consumers.

The crisis prompted several countries in Southeast Asia to announce plans to expand or extend EV tax incentives as part of their response. Vietnam, already the largest EV market in the region, moved to solidify its position. The energy security benefits proved particularly compelling for oil-importing nations, with China leading the way by avoiding consumption of approximately 1 million barrels of oil per day through its electric vehicle fleet in 2025.

Electric Trucks Emerge as Major Growth Segment

While passenger vehicles dominated headlines, the electric truck market posted extraordinary growth in 2025. Global electric truck sales more than doubled compared to 2024, reaching 9% of all truck sales worldwide. China drove the vast majority of this expansion, with sales doubling for the second consecutive year. One in four trucks sold in China carried electric powertrains by year's end.

The total cost of ownership for electric trucks achieved competitiveness in China thanks to falling battery prices and lower operating costs, even though purchase prices remained two to three times higher than diesel equivalents. European projections suggest total cost of ownership parity for electric trucks will arrive by 2030, supporting continued growth. The European Union already hosts over 1,000 charging points dedicated exclusively to electric trucks, enabling long-distance electric trucking operations.

New electric truck producers from the machinery and heavy industry sectors captured market share in China, with nearly 30% of the Chinese electric truck market going to new entrants that lack conventional models in their product lines. Chinese electric truck sales came almost exclusively from Chinese manufacturers using Chinese batteries, with CATL supplying 80% of the total, reflecting a highly integrated domestic ecosystem.

Battery Technology and Manufacturing Reshape Industry

Battery cell production remained heavily concentrated in 2025, with China accounting for over 80% of global output and even higher shares of active materials production. Nearly all battery cells used worldwide came from companies headquartered in China, Korea, or Japan, though the market share of Chinese producers grew especially rapidly in the European Union, nearly doubling since 2023.

Despite lithium-ion battery manufacturing capacity growing faster in the European Union and United States than in China during the year, projections suggest China will remain the largest producer of batteries and battery materials through 2035 based on stated policies. Narrow profit margins put pressure on some battery manufacturers, creating an industry shake-out that may accelerate consolidation.

Battery technology continued advancing rapidly, with patents related to batteries accounting for nearly half of all energy sector patents. The first 1,000-volt models appeared in 2025, enabling charging times under 10 minutes in some cases. New power electronics materials, battery cell technologies, and pack architectures enabled more efficient, higher-voltage, and faster charging systems. The number of electric cars capable of using chargers above 250 kilowatts remained below 5% of the vehicle stock, but sales grew alongside the expansion of ultra-fast and megawatt-scale chargers.

Software and Artificial Intelligence Transform Vehicle Design

Following the lead of pure-play EV makers, most major automakers began developing vehicles with more centralized software systems allowing key functions and systems to be updated remotely. Battery electric vehicles emerged as the most advanced examples of these software-defined vehicles, which rely on more centralized control architectures enabling a wide range of developments supported by falling sensor prices, more powerful computing chips, and artificial intelligence applications.

Advanced driver assistance systems, including automated steering and speed control, represented key applications alongside EV battery management improvements. The deployment of autonomous vehicles accelerated, with driverless taxis, all of them electric, now operating commercially in more than 20 cities, mainly in China and the United States.

The greater number of semiconductors needed to support increasingly digital and autonomous vehicles created growing reliance on supply chains that are already geographically concentrated. Managing cybersecurity risks emerged as an increasingly important challenge for automakers as connectivity and automation expanded.

Charging Infrastructure Expands Globally

Private charging infrastructure reached an estimated 43 million light-duty vehicle charging points globally in 2025, supporting an electric vehicle stock of around 76 million. About one-third of private charging points existed in China, one-third in Europe, and one in six in the United States.

Home charging remained the preferred method for those with access, due to its relative affordability and convenience. Access varied significantly by housing type and region. In Norway, where 64% of the population lives in detached or semi-detached houses, around 90% of EV owners could charge at home. In China, where only 7% of residents live in single-family houses, approximately 50% of EV owners had home chargers, though another third accessed shared residential chargers.

Policy measures supporting home charging access included building regulations in many countries. The European Union revised its Energy Performance of Buildings Directive in 2024 to require new or renovated buildings to include pre-cabling for EV charging. Kenya's 2024 National Building Code mandated 5% of parking spaces in all new buildings be equipped for EV charging, while India's Model Building Bye-Laws called for charging infrastructure covering 20% of parking capacity.

Vehicle-to-Grid Technology Offers Grid Flexibility Potential

The first commercial offers for vehicle-to-grid services for private EV owners appeared in 2025, allowing electric vehicles to feed electricity back to the grid during peak demand periods. This technology promised to help manage grid capacity constraints as EV deployment and charging speeds increased. However, few vehicle-to-grid capable models were available, the regulatory landscape remained fragmented, and standards had not yet achieved clarity.

Smart charging, which reduces peak demand by shifting charging loads to off-peak hours, offered additional grid management opportunities. These measures gained importance as projections showed electricity demand from EVs could exceed 1,500 terawatt-hours by 2035, growing around sixfold from 2025 levels based on current policies.

Two and Three-Wheelers Continue Electrification Leadership

The most electrified road transport segment, two and three-wheelers, continued expanding in 2025. While sales in China and India, the world's largest two-wheeler markets, grew only slightly to a total of 8.4 million units, sales doubled in Vietnam, underpinning global growth. African sales grew markedly to reach about 70,000 two-wheelers in 2025, more than 80 times the volume at the decade's start.

Electric three-wheelers maintained a sales share of over 25%, continuing to increase even as the overall three-wheeler market contracted. These smaller vehicles offered particularly compelling economics for emerging markets, with lower purchase prices and operating costs making electric mobility accessible to a broader population.

2026 Forecast Points to Continued Acceleration

Global electric car sales are expected to grow to 23 million in 2026, representing 28% of total car sales. Europe appears poised for the largest growth among major markets, with sales projected to increase by around 20%, bringing the share to one in three cars sold. China's electric car sales are set to continue growing, albeit at a slower pace than previous years, to reach almost 60% of total car sales.

Sales across Asia Pacific countries other than China are expected to grow by over 50%, while Latin American sales are projected to rise by 45%. The wider economic impacts of the ongoing Middle East conflict might temper overall car sales, but in many regions, upside potential exists depending on how, when, and which policies are enacted in response to the energy crisis.

First quarter 2026 data revealed a complex picture. Global sales of around 3.9 million units came in 8% lower than the same period in 2025, primarily because of lower sales in China and the United States following key policy changes. However, this overall decline masked strong growth in many countries.

European sales climbed close to 30% year-on-year, countries in Asia Pacific excluding China saw year-on-year sales growth of 80%, and Latin American sales rose by 75%. Around 30 countries recorded record-breaking monthly sales in March 2026, with a further 60 countries posting year-on-year sales growth.

Preliminary April data showed monthly electric car sales in China growing to a record high of over 60% of total car sales, even as year-to-date figures remained lower than 2025 levels, suggesting a strong recovery from earlier slowdowns.

Long-Term Outlook Envisions Transport Transformation

Looking toward 2035, projections suggest the global fleet of electric vehicles will grow more than sixfold from 2025 levels to reach as many as 510 million units, excluding electric two and three-wheelers. The increasing cost-competitiveness of EVs, combined with tighter CO2 and fuel economy standards, will drive market growth, pushing the share of EVs in global car sales to around 50% by 2035 in the IEA's exploratory scenarios.

The share of conventional internal combustion engine cars continues shrinking in all scenarios, with sales never returning to their 2017 peak. In China, the trajectory points toward electric vehicles exceeding 90% of total car sales by 2035. European CO2 standards will continue driving sales, with the proposed Automotive Package potentially moderating the 2035 outlook while still seeing electric car sales shares exceed 90%.

Global annual oil displacement by electric vehicles is projected to triple to around 5 million barrels per day by 2030, with China accounting for 2.7 million barrels per day. By 2035, electric vehicles worldwide could displace approximately 9 million barrels of oil per day in the Current Policies Scenario, with China representing roughly half of the global total displacement. Growing deployment of electric trucks will contribute significantly, avoiding consumption of 1 million barrels per day by 2035.

Trade Dynamics Reshape Global Automotive Industry

Trade patterns continued evolving dramatically in 2025, with around one-quarter of electric cars produced being traded between countries. China overtook the European Union to become the largest car exporter in 2024, and the gap widened in 2025 as Chinese exports doubled. More than 35% of China's car exports were electric vehicles, up from 20% in 2024.

Imports from China accounted for 55% of electric car sales in 2025 in countries outside Europe and the United States, up from less than 5% just five years earlier. More than half of electric cars sold in Southeast Asia came from Chinese brands, while one-third came from a Vietnamese manufacturer. European Union electric car exports grew 25% in 2025, but imports also rose by around 35% year-on-year to more than 900,000 units, with China accounting for almost 60% of these imports.

In the first quarter of 2026, electric car exports from China more than doubled compared with the same period in 2025, offsetting weaker domestic sales. However, Chinese exports could face headwinds as inventories accumulated. Estimates suggest exports exceeded overseas sales by more than 25% in 2025, pointing to potential market adjustments ahead.

Policy Responses Will Shape Future Trajectory

The current high oil price environment draws consumer attention to the economic benefits of driving electric vehicles. Electric cars generally have lower running costs than internal combustion engine vehicles, mainly due to their higher efficiency, and the recent rise in oil prices resulting from the Middle East conflict has further increased the cost savings associated with driving an EV.

Oil-importing emerging and developing economies across the world have some of the strongest incentives to implement policies to further accelerate electric car adoption. These include countries in Southeast Asia such as Thailand, Latin America such as Chile, and Africa such as South Africa. In the short term, this could be achieved by increasing imports of affordable Chinese electric cars, while in the longer term, incentivizing domestic supply could offer an additional pathway.

The road transport sector's close to half share of total oil demand positions policy responses to the current crisis to shape the global car market for years to come. The oil crisis of the 1970s prompted introduction of fuel efficiency standards that nearly doubled the fuel economy of conventional cars between 1975 and today. During the COVID-19 pandemic, many countries introduced EV subsidies to boost uptake and support broader economic recovery. The current energy crisis appears poised to trigger a similar wave of policy innovation focused on accelerating the transition to electric mobility.

The transformation extends beyond passenger vehicles to encompass trucks, buses, and two and three-wheelers, creating a comprehensive shift in road transport. Combined with advancing battery technology, expanding charging infrastructure, growing manufacturing capacity, and evolving trade patterns, the electric vehicle revolution appears to have reached an inflection point where momentum becomes self-sustaining in an growing number of markets worldwide.

As the industry navigates challenges including supply chain concentration, cybersecurity risks, grid integration requirements, and evolving policy frameworks, the fundamental trajectory appears established. The question for most markets has shifted from whether electric vehicles will dominate to when that dominance will be achieved and how the transition will be managed to maximize economic, environmental, and energy security benefits.

entry.title: iCAUR 03T Electric SUV Arrives
entry.summary: iCAUR South Africa has officially launched the 03T electric SUV, bringing a new contender to the country's expanding new-energy vehicle market. The model, positioned above the brand's existing V23 in the local lineup, goes on…
entry.content:
iCAUR South Africa has officially launched the 03T electric SUV, bringing a new contender to the country's expanding new-energy vehicle market. The model, positioned above the brand's existing V23 in the local lineup, goes on sale in South African showrooms from 28 May 2026 and is priced from R639,900.

The 03T is the latest offering from iCAUR, the new-energy sub-brand operating under the Chery Global umbrella. It arrives in two derivatives — a rear-wheel-drive 2WD and an all-wheel-drive AWD — giving buyers a choice between efficient single-motor performance and more capable dual-motor output.

The 2WD variant is powered by a single rear-mounted electric motor producing 135 kW and 220 N.m of torque, drawing from a 65.69 kWh battery. It accelerates from 0 to 100 km/h in 10.5 seconds and returns an NEDC-estimated range of 431 km at a consumption rate of 18.3 kWh/100 km.

The AWD derivative pairs a dual-motor setup for a combined output of 205 kW and 385 N.m, supported by a slightly larger 69.77 kWh battery. It covers the 0 to 100 km/h sprint in 6.5 seconds and offers an NEDC-estimated range of 436 km at 19.9 kWh/100 km. Both variants are limited to a top speed of 150 km/h and can be charged from 10% to 80% via DC fast charging in 30 minutes.

Bold Proportions and a Well-Appointed Cabin

Visually, the 03T adopts a squared-off, upright stance with pronounced wheel arches and slim LED lighting elements. Its all-aluminium multi-cavity cage body is engineered for corrosion resistance of up to 30 years, while reducing vehicle weight by more than 30% and lowering energy consumption by 3%.

A panoramic glass sunroof and 19-inch alloy wheels wrapped in 245/55 tyres complete the exterior. Five paint options are available, spanning Khaki White, Carbon Crystal Black, Cyan Grey, Starlight Silver, and Toronto Red.

Inside, the 03T seats five across a 2,715 mm wheelbase, with 450 litres of boot space that expands to 1,238 litres with the 60:40 split-folding rear seats lowered. A rear storage box adds a further 40 litres.

Both trims feature a 15.6-inch touchscreen, wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, voice command functionality, a 540-degree surround-view camera, and a 50-watt wireless charger. The 2WD is fitted with an eight-speaker audio system, while the AWD upgrades to a 12-speaker Infinity setup.

Seat specification on the 2WD includes black leather upholstery, climate control, ambient lighting, and electrically adjustable heated and ventilated front seats with four-way lumbar support. AWD buyers gain a massage function for front occupants and an electrically adjustable passenger leg rest.

Safety and Ownership Support

The 03T carries six airbags across both trims, alongside a full suite of active driver assistance systems. These include Automatic Emergency Braking with vehicle, pedestrian and bicycle recognition, Adaptive Cruise Control, Lane Departure Warning and Prevention, Blind Spot Detection, and Traffic Jam Assist, among others. Front and rear parking sensors and ISOFIX anchorage points are standard throughout the range.

Shannon Gahagan, National Brand and Marketing Manager at iCAUR South Africa, described the 03T as a clear expression of the brand's identity. "Its design gives it a distinctive presence, but the real strength of the 03T is how it combines that personality with comfort, space, safety, and a choice of electric drivetrains suited to different customer needs," she said.

Both models are backed by an eight-year/200,000 km vehicle warranty, an eight-year/160,000 km power battery warranty for the first owner, a five-year/100,000 km service plan, and eight-year/200,000 km roadside assistance.

At R639,900 for the 2WD and R699,900 for the AWD, the 03T's pricing is particularly keen when compared to the plug-in hybrids from Jetour.
